newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin faces more tests before heart surgery.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin faces more tests before heart surgery.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin is spending two more days in hospital for tests ahead of planned heart surgery, the Kremlin said on Monday, as speculation continued over who will control Russia's nuclear trigger during the operation.

The presidential press office said Yeltsin, who went into Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital for tests on Friday, would spend two further days there but gave no details of what tests would be carried out.

It also gave no reason for the apparent extension to Yelstin's stay -- spokesmen original said he would spend the weekend at the hospital -- sparking further speculation about the true state of the 65-year-old president's health.
First lady Naina Yeltsin is convalescing after a kidney operation at the same clinic last month.
Yeltsin, who suffered two heart attacks last year, ended months of equivocation over his health, and a Kremlin tradition of secrecy, when he announced on September 5 that he needed cardiac surgery.

Doctors have said Yeltsin will undergo a bypass operation to improve blood flow to the heart but have not given a date for the treatment. Yeltsin had originally said the operation would probably be at the end of the month.

Despite the new policy of openness, details of how, when and to whom Yeltsin will hand over the "nuclear button", which authorises the launch of Russia's atomic weapons, remain hazy. It is not even certain that he will relinquish the device.

Yeltsin's spokesman said last week the president was considering handing over power briefly and giving up control of the button, which accompanies the chief-of-staff everywhere in a black briefcase, around the time of the operation. But he did not say to whom.
Under the constitution, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin would take over if Yeltsin were incapacitated. But the law does not set out a procedure for handing over the nuclear briefcase.
There has been no suggestion that any of the senior officials to whom the button could be entrusted would be more likely to press it.

But the issue of control over the button, which sends coded instructions to military commanders in charge of nuclear weapons, has highlighted speculation over a power struggle at the summit of power in Russia.
"Today the nuclear briefcase has become a symbol of power, just as the orb and sceptre once were," commercial NTV television's current affairs programme Itogi said on Sunday.
"Not only has no procedure (for handing over the nuclear button) been worked out, but no law has been written for it," correspondent Vadim Glusker said.

Itogi said it had learned from Kremlin sources that Yeltsin would sign a decree handing over the nuclear button to Chernomyrdin for a short time but reassume it as soon as he came round after the operation.
U.S. President Bill Clinton called Yeltsin on Sunday to wish him well with the operation.
"It was just a (friendly) call to talk about his pending surgery and to wish him luck," White House spokeswoman Mary Ellen Glynn told reporters with Clinton in Iowa.
